title: Second US Deportation Flight Carrying Iranians Turns Back in Three Days
excerpt: A charter flight carrying at least nine Iranian deportees out of Mesa, Arizona, turned back about 30 minutes after takeoff early Tuesday after Pakistan declined to accept the group, The New York Times reported. It was the second failed removal attempt in three days.
body:
• A US deportation flight carrying Iranians bound for Iran via Pakistan turned back and landed in Arizona early Tuesday, the second failed attempt in three days, according to The New York Times reporting cited by Newsmax.
  • The flight reversed course after Pakistan abruptly declined to accept the group, a US official and a detainee's relative told the Times; at least nine people were aboard.
  • On Sunday, a separate flight was cancelled after at least eight Iranians had already boarded in Mesa, an attorney for some detainees told the Associated Press.
  • A federal judge has ordered the government to give 24 hours' notice of any finalised plan to deport Iranians and five days' written notice before a removal is carried out.

A US deportation flight carrying Iranians bound for Iran via Pakistan turned back and landed in Arizona early on Tuesday, the second failed attempt in three days to send Iranians home amid the US-Iran war, according to reporting by The New York Times cited by Newsmax.

The flight reversed course after Pakistan abruptly declined to accept the group, the Times reported, citing a US official and a relative of one detainee who said an Iranian official relayed that account. The relative told the Times at least nine people were aboard, and that they were back in an Arizona immigration detention facility by Tuesday afternoon. Human Rights First, a Washington nonprofit that tracks deportation flights, said the small charter jet left Mesa, Arizona, just before 5 a.m., turned around about 30 minutes later and landed back at the same Immigration and Customs Enforcement staging site, according to the Times.

Sunday's Cancelled Flight

The scrapped Tuesday trip followed a Sunday attempt in which at least eight Iranians boarded a plane in Mesa for a flight routed through the country of Georgia to Pakistan, and were then taken off when the flight was cancelled without explanation. Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions for some of the detainees, gave that account to the Associated Press. Court filings by the fund said 11 Iranian nationals — 10 men and one woman — had been scheduled for removal on the flight.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to confirm either operation, saying it does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules and passenger details.

The Court Battle Behind the Flights

The removals are the subject of a lawsuit before US District Judge Ana Reyes in Washington, who has ordered the government to give the court 24 hours' notice of any finalised plan to deport Iranians and five days' written notice before any removal is carried out. The lawsuit, filed in July, alleges the government unlawfully shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the United States with Iranian officials. The fund has urged authorities to halt deportations to Iran during the war, warning returnees could face persecution, torture or death.

A Route With No Direct Path

The United States cannot fly removal charters directly into Tehran: it has no diplomatic relations with Iran. According to the Times, the administration is planning at least two operations this month to deport people to Afghanistan and Iran using Pakistan as the transfer point. Three deportation flights between September 2025 and January 2026 removed more than 100 Iranians, according to the AP.

Tuesday's turnback shows the fragility of that workaround. The route depends on a third country accepting the transfer, and this time — on the Times' account — Pakistan declined after the plane was already in the air. The detainees are back in detention in Arizona, and any further attempt will again run through both the transit country's consent and the notice requirements Judge Reyes has imposed.
